paragraphs: Bank of Ireland is using more artificial intelligence, or AI. AI is computer software that can learn. Many banks now use it.
The bank uses AI to find scams. It has checked about 2.9 million payments with AI.
The bank also has an AI tool called the benefits finder. People used it 31,000 times. It found €55 million in tax money that customers may get back.
Almost 7,000 workers at the bank have learned to use AI. Some of them save half an hour every day.
Fraud is a growing problem in Ireland. Last year, people lost €179 million in fraud payments. In 2024, it was €141 million.
Bank of Ireland says it is using artificial intelligence (AI) more and more, especially to stop fraud and to help customers with their money.

The bank's scam detection system, which uses AI, has checked around 2.9 million customer payments. Prag Sharma, who became the bank's chief AI officer on 1 October, says the bank wants to use the technology widely but safely.

In April, the bank started a tool called the benefits finder. It has been used 31,000 times and has found €55 million in tax refunds that customers could claim. Last year, the bank also gave customers 127 million AI-based tips about their spending.

AI is changing work inside the bank too. Almost 7,000 staff have done training in tools like Microsoft Copilot, and some save up to 30 minutes a day. In the call centre, the number of calls passed to another person has fallen by more than 40 per cent.
The news comes as fraud grows in Ireland. Central Bank figures show that fraudulent payments rose from €141 million in 2024 to €179 million in 2025.

Bank of Ireland says it is accelerating the use of artificial intelligence across its business, with the technology now built into its fraud detection systems and its financial guidance for customers.

According to the bank, its AI-powered scam detection technology has assessed roughly 2.9 million customer transactions. Prag Sharma, who was appointed chief AI officer on October 1st, said there was a strong drive within the organisation to adopt the technology safely.

A generative AI tool called the benefits finder, launched in April, has been used 31,000 times and has identified €55 million in potential tax refunds for customers. The bank also provided 127 million AI-generated spending insights last year.

Internally, almost 7,000 employees have completed training on tools such as Microsoft Copilot, saving some staff up to half an hour a day. Call transfers in the contact centre have fallen by more than 40 per cent.

The push comes against a backdrop of rising fraud. Central Bank data shows reported fraudulent transactions in the State climbed from €141 million in 2024 to €179 million in 2025, equivalent to about one in every 10,000 payments.

Bank of Ireland is ramping up its deployment of artificial intelligence, embedding the technology in its fraud detection software and harnessing it to offer customers insights into their financial wellbeing.

The lender says its AI-driven scam detection tools have scrutinised some 2.9 million customer transactions. Prag Sharma, who took up the role of chief AI officer at the start of October, spoke of a concerted push to roll out the technology across the bank without compromising safety.

Among the more eye-catching initiatives is the benefits finder, a generative AI tool unveiled in April. It has been consulted 31,000 times and has flagged €55 million in tax refunds that customers may be entitled to reclaim.

Behind the scenes, nearly 7,000 staff have been trained on assistants such as Microsoft Copilot, with some reclaiming up to half an hour of their working day, while transfers between contact centre agents have been slashed by over 40 per cent.

The drive unfolds amid an escalating fraud problem: Central Bank figures show reported fraudulent transactions swelled from €141 million in 2024 to €179 million last year, roughly one in every 10,000 payments.

Bank of Ireland has announced that it is accelerating the integration of artificial intelligence into its operations, most notably in the detection of fraud and the provision of financial guidance to customers.

The institution reports that its AI-based scam detection system has evaluated approximately 2.9 million customer transactions. According to Prag Sharma, who assumed the position of chief AI officer on 1 October, the organisation is committed to adopting the technology extensively, albeit in a responsible manner.

Furthermore, a generative AI application known as the benefits finder, introduced in April, has been utilised 31,000 times and has identified a substantial €55 million in potential tax refunds. In addition, the bank generated 127 million automated spending insights for customers in the previous year.

The technology has also had considerable implications for internal productivity. Almost 7,000 employees have received training in tools such as Microsoft Copilot, which has enabled some to save up to thirty minutes daily, while call transfers within the contact centre have decreased by more than 40 per cent.

These developments must be considered in the context of a significant rise in financial crime. Data from the Central Bank indicate that reported fraudulent transactions increased from €141 million in 2024 to €179 million in 2025, equivalent to approximately one in every 10,000 payments.

A generative AI tool called the benefits finder, launched in April, has been used 31,000 times and has identified €55 million in potential tax refunds for customers. The bank also provided 127 million AI-generated spending insights last year.

Internally, almost 7,000 employees have completed training on tools such as Microsoft Copilot, saving some staff up to half an hour a day. Call transfers in the contact centre have fallen by more than 40 per cent.

The push comes against a backdrop of rising fraud. Central Bank data shows reported fraudulent transactions in the State climbed from €141 million in 2024 to €179 million in 2025, equivalent to about one in every 10,000 payments.
